Hay's diplomatic triumph in China lifted Adams's spirits, but King's collapse and Hay's failing health darkened the season; meanwhile the magnet on Adams's desk, and the geologists' confessions of ignorance, warned him that the unity he had sought all his life was dissolving into a multiplicity science could no longer pretend to govern.

# CHAPTER XXVII

TEUFELSDRÖCKH
(1901)

Inevitable Paris beckoned. Even more vigorously than in the twelfth century, Paris taught in the twentieth; but science had got quite beyond his horizon, and mathematics had become the only necessary language of thought. The mass and originality of the city's product would have swamped any previous age, as it very nearly swamped its own; the effect was chaos, and Adams stood as helpless before it as before the chaos of New York. His single thought was to keep in front of the movement, and, if necessary, lead it to chaos, but never fall behind.

Baireuth, promised himself for thirty years, came at last. In 1876 the rococo setting had seemed correct atmosphere for Siegfried and Brünhilde; in 1901 Wagner had become a part of the world, as familiar as Shakespeare, and New York knew better than Baireuth what he meant. Paris coquetted with catastrophe as though it were an old mistress; New York met it with a glow of fascinated horror, like an inevitable earthquake. Flattery had lost its charm, but the Fluch-motif went home.

Russia next, for as inertia she represented three-fourths of the human race, and her movement might be the true movement of the future against the hasty and unsure acceleration of America. From the first glimpse of the Polish Jew at the accidental railway station, in all his weird horror, to the last vision of the Russian peasant kissing his ikon before the railway Virgin at St. Petersburg, all was logical, conservative, Christian, and anarchic. Russia became luminous like the salt of radium; but with a negative luminosity, as though she were a substance whose energies had been sucked out — an inert residuum — with movement of pure inertia. One peasant kissing an ikon on a saint's day served for a hundred million. He assumed a slow acceleration that would, at a generation's end, leave the gap between east and west relatively the same.

Then north — Stockholm, Trondhjem, and the mail-steamer to Hammerfest, where seventy years before a futile Carlylean Teufelsdröckh had stopped to ask futile questions of the silent infinite. The infinite seemed to have become loquacious, chattering gossip in one's ear. Electric lighting and telephones led tourists close up to the polar ice-cap, beyond the level of the magnetic pole; and there the newer Teufelsdröckh sat dumb with surprise. Day by day, far within the realm of night, the news had come — an attempt on McKinley's life, the President's condition, the doings of Hay and Roosevelt, until a little journal announced his death. The electro-dynamo-social universe worked better than the sun. The acceleration was marvellous, and wholly in the lines of unity. Yet the nightmare of the glacial ice-cap still pressed down from the hills, ready at any moment to advance, and Adams felt the emotion of his Norwegian fishermen ancestors, jammed with their faces to the sea, the ice on the north, the ice-cap of Russian inertia pressing from behind. He had never before met a ne plus ultra.

South again to Hamburg, Bremen, Cologne — a Germany new to mankind. Hamburg was almost as American as St. Louis; Düsseldorf had taken on the sooty grime of Birmingham; Cologne was a railway centre whose finished cathedral bore the absent-minded air of a cathedral of Chicago. In 1858 the whole plain of northern Europe had borne evident marks of being still the prehistoric highway between Asia and the ocean; in 1901 Russia had vanished, and not even France was felt. Coal alone was felt. From Hammerfest to Cherbourg on one shore of the ocean, from Halifax to Norfolk on the other, one great empire was ruled by one great emperor — Coal. Beyond lay Russia, and there an older, perhaps a surer, power, resting on the eternal law of inertia, held its own.

The relative value of the two powers became more interesting every year; for the mass of Russian inertia was moving irresistibly over China, and John Hay stood in its path. As long as de Witte ruled, Hay was safe. Should de Witte fall, Hay would totter.
